links.took: Atari's two-paddle ball-and-volley rally rules and quick arcade scoring.
links.added: Packed 50 paddle-game variations for up to four players onto an Atari 2600 launch cartridge.
links.extra: Programmed by Joe Decuir as one of nine Atari 2600 launch cartridges in September 1977.

links.took: Bouncing a ball off a sliding paddle to chip through rows of colored overhead bricks.
links.added: Introduced Progressive advancing walls, Double stacked paddles, and Cavity multi-ball liberation modes.
links.extra: Designed at Atari by Ed Rotberg and Ed Logg.

links.took: Pocket LCD timing gameplay, digital clock hardware, and simple reflexes built by Gunpei Yokoi's R&D1.
links.added: Folded two screens into a clamshell casing and debuted Nintendo's cross-shaped directional pad.
links.extra: Ball launched Nintendo's handheld line in April 1980; Donkey Kong's 1982 D-pad later defined console controllers.

links.took: Gunpei Yokoi and Satoru Okada's portable LCD hardware craft focused on battery life and pick-up play.
links.added: Swapped fixed LCD segments for interchangeable Game Boy cartridges and a full scrolling Mario adventure.
links.extra: Both games came out of Nintendo R&D1 under Gunpei Yokoi and Satoru Okada.

links.took: Mario climbing girders, leaping over rolling barrels, and rescuing Pauline from Donkey Kong.
links.added: Split the climb across two clamshell LCD screens and replaced the arcade joystick with a flat D-pad.

src.t: Wikipedia: List of LCD games featuring Mario
KMUW, Gunpei Yokoi and the Game & Watch D-pad, Oct 2016

links.extra: Its dual-screen clamshell also prefigured the Nintendo DS two decades later.

links.took: Swooping alien attack formations and colorful fixed-screen space shooting.
links.added: Added regenerating bird enemies, a brief protective shield, and a multi-layered mothership boss fight.
links.extra: Early arcade shooter credited with introducing a dedicated end-of-loop mothership boss encounter.

links.took: Rotary paddle deflection and chipping through layered defensive brick walls with bouncing projectiles.
links.added: Turned solo brick-breaking into four corner fortresses defending kings against simultaneous multiplayer fireballs.
links.extra: Conceived by Atari designer Roger Hector and ported to Atari 2600 by Carla Meninsky.

links.took: Single-screen corridor maze gunfights against patrolling foes paired with taunting synthesized arcade speech.
links.added: Added simultaneous two-player co-op or friendly-fire betrayal, radar tracking, invisible monsters, and a teleporting boss.
links.extra: Prototyped as Invisible Monsters in 1980 by Dave Nutting Associates before its Midway arcade release.

links.took: Popularized simultaneous multiplayer monster-hunting inside walled arcade mazes with ranged attacks.
links.added: Scaled arena skirmishes to four-player scrolling fantasy dungeons with distinct classes and monster generators.
links.extra: Helped bridge single-screen maze shooters and multi-player arcade dungeon crawlers.

links.took: The MIT mainframe dungeon's prose, puzzles, underground lamp exploration, and rich verb parser.
links.added: Split the massive mainframe game into a commercial home-computer episode running on Infocom's portable Z-machine.

src.t: Dave Lebling, Classic Game Postmortem: Zork, GDC Vault, Mar 2014

links.extra: Infocom's Z-machine interpreter let Zork I ship across Apple II, DOS, C64, Mac, and Amiga.

links.took: Home-computer text adventure exploration built around parsing typed commands across interconnected locations.
links.added: Added compressed room illustrations, the Inglish full-sentence parser, object weight physics, and independent real-time NPCs.
links.extra: Created by Veronika Megler and Philip Mitchell at Beam Software for Melbourne House.

links.took: Namco's omnidirectional scrolling hardware board and side-mounted radar tracking distant targets.
links.added: Moved scrolling chases into open space with dual front-and-rear cannons, voice alerts, and rotating starbases.
links.extra: Designed by Seiichi Sato at Namco specifically to reuse Rally-X arcade circuit boards.

links.took: David Crane's crisp Atari 2600 sprite animation routines and split-second obstacle-timing design at Activision.
links.added: Expanded single-screen highway sprints into a 255-screen flip-screen jungle adventure with vines, pits, and treasures.
links.extra: David Crane coded Freeway in July 1981 before building Pitfall! the following year.

links.took: Popularized steering a chicken across multi-lane highways of speeding traffic for timed high scores.
links.added: Blended endless lane-dodging chicken sprints with Frogger's river logs, voxel art, and collectible characters.
links.extra: David Crane conceived Freeway independently in 1981 after dodging traffic on Chicago's Lake Shore Drive.

links.took: Popularized precision horizontal sliding with the Atari 2600 rotary paddle controller.
links.added: Replaced brick walls with three water buckets catching accelerating bombs dropped by an animated Mad Bomber.

src.t: Game Developer, The History of Activision, Jul 2007

links.extra: Larry Kaplan openly adapted Atari's 1978 arcade game Avalanche while David Crane drew the expressive bomber.

links.took: Popularized steering a continuous trail across an open arcade rectangle without colliding into lines.
links.added: Turned trail-drawing into territory capture enclosing an erratic line creature with fast-draw and risky slow-draw multipliers.
links.extra: Designed by husband-and-wife team Randy and Sandy Pfeiffer for Taito.

links.took: Wraparound horizontal planet defense, scanner radar, smart bombs, and rescuing falling humanoids.
links.added: Introduced an Inviso cloaking button, mid-screen Stargate warps to endangered humanoids, and deadlier alien waves.
links.extra: Created by Eugene Jarvis and Larry DeMar at Vid Kidz; later retitled Defender II on home consoles.

links.took: Sega's fast traffic-weaving Formula racing loop across changing road environments.
links.added: Shifted to a behind-the-car 2.5D view with scaling sprites, weather shifts, and dusk-to-night lighting transitions.
links.extra: Designed and programmed solo by Steve Hanawa on Sega's VCO Object arcade board.

links.took: Rear-view third-person arcade racing using scaling roadside objects and traffic-passing speed.
links.added: Introduced smooth curved track geometry modeled on Fuji Speedway, qualifying laps, and realistic steering physics.
links.extra: Turbo debuted behind-the-car scaling-sprite racing one year before Namco's Pole Position.

links.took: Popularized single-screen arcade platform climbing while dodging tumbling hazards and patrolling enemies.
links.added: Moved hopping onto an isometric cube pyramid where diagonal jumps flip block colors under Coily's pursuit.
links.extra: Created by Warren Davis and Jeff Lee at Gottlieb with a diagonally mounted four-way joystick.

links.took: Isometric diagonal hopping across stacked blocks with bottomless drop-offs and chasing hazards.
links.added: Expanded cube-hopping into eleven scrolling NES obstacle courses where eating pellets lengthens your snake tail.
links.extra: Combined Q*bert's isometric leaps with Rare's Marble Madness NES conversion engine.

links.took: Chipping through rotating concentric energy barriers to strike an enemy cannon hidden inside.
links.added: Rebuilt the duel horizontally for Atari 2600 with a shield-nibbling fly, safe Neutral Zone, and Zorlon Cannon.

src.t: Howard Scott Warshaw interview, Atari Newsroom, May 2024
Game Developer, Howard Scott Warshaw GDC Postmortem, Dec 2014

links.extra: Began as an Atari 2600 conversion of Cinematronics' vector arcade hit before Warshaw pitched an original pivot.

links.took: Single-screen arcade shooting centered on eroding defensive barriers before destroying the foe behind them.
links.added: Rotated the duel horizontally with 360-degree flight, a static-filled Neutral Zone, and a charged super-shot.
links.extra: Became Atari's best-selling original Atari 2600 cartridge.

links.took: Forced-scrolling canyon raids where blowing up ground fuel tanks keeps your ship airborne.
links.added: Pioneered isometric scrolling where cast shadows and an altimeter govern flying over fortress walls.
links.extra: Developed by Sega with Ikegami Tsushinki, the contract studio that programmed Donkey Kong.

links.took: A 60-degree diagonal isometric scrolling street perspective showing depth and approaching obstacles.
links.added: Traded space combat for steering a BMX with handlebars, tossing newspapers to subscribers while dodging suburbia.

src.t: John Salwitz, Making of Atari's Paperboy, Thumbsticks

links.extra: John Salwitz and Dave Ralston built Paperboy on Atari System 2 hardware.

links.took: Popularized high-speed timed street deliveries weaving past chaotic urban traffic and pedestrians.
links.added: Moved frantic arcade errands into a sunny 3D open city with drifting cabs, stunt ramps, and fares.
links.extra: Bridged 1980s route-delivery coin-ops and 3D arcade driving sandboxes.

links.took: Atari's 3D wireframe vector engine and dual-handle yoke developed for its military Battlezone simulator.
links.added: Added color vector Tie Fighters, digitized film voices, and a three-phase Death Star trench run.
links.extra: Designed by Mike Hally; its flight yoke reused tooling from Atari's Army Battlezone trainer.

links.took: First-person cockpit X-Wing combat against Tie Fighters culminating in the Death Star trench run.
links.added: Replaced on-rails wireframe waves with free-roaming 3D space missions, shield-weapon power routing, and Rebel campaigns.
links.extra: Carried Atari's 1983 cockpit fantasy into 1990s PC space simulation.

links.took: Popularized fixed-screen platform navigation dodging enemies across floating ledges for escalating score runs.
links.added: Replaced ladder climbing with soaring high jumps, rapid mid-air gliding, and sequential lit-bomb score bonuses.
links.extra: Created by Michitaka Tsuruta and Kazutoshi Ueda at Tehkan.

links.took: Open-ended fantasy questing across named landmarks, items, and storied perils.
links.added: Fused adventure exploration with army wargaming across 4,000 first-person panoramic 'landscaping' views.
links.extra: Written solo by Mike Singleton on the ZX Spectrum with dual quest and military victory paths.

links.took: Two-player cooperative-or-mischievous platforming centered on bumping overhead blocks to knock foes loose.
links.added: Turned single-screen pipes into vertically scrolling icy mountains climbed with mallets and bonus-peak condors.
links.extra: Produced by Shigeru Miyamoto and Masayuki Uemura with Mario Bros. programmer Toshihiko Nakago.

links.took: Programmer Kazuaki Morita's early NES jump-physics and scrolling tile practice under Nintendo's core team.
links.added: Refined momentum jumping and smooth horizontal scrolling across eight sprawling Mushroom Kingdom worlds.
links.extra: Released in January 1985; Morita called Ice Climber his warm-up before programming Super Mario Bros.

links.took: Popularized laying timed explosive traps across interconnected rooms to outsmart opponents.
links.added: Introduced simultaneous 'Simulvision' split-screen espionage duels where rivals booby-trap furniture and race to escape.

src.t: Wikipedia: Spy vs. Spy (1984 video game)

links.extra: Programmed by Mike Riedel at First Star Software, pioneering competitive split-screen mind games.

links.took: Nintendo R&D1's Famicom Disk System engine, physics routines, password structure, and even Metroid-like Komayto foes.
links.added: Swapped sci-fi corridors for Greek-myth vertical climbing, weapon shops, eggplant curses, and maze fortresses.

src.t: Nintendo World Report, Making of a Myth: Kid Icarus, Mar 2012

links.extra: Metroid shipped in August 1986; Yoshio Sakamoto and the Metroid team then helped Toru Osawa finish Kid Icarus by December.

links.took: Popularized climbing multi-story arcade structures featuring a giant gorilla fending off hazards.
links.added: Let up to three players control giant movie monsters climbing and punching entire city skyscrapers to rubble.
links.extra: Designed by Brian Colin and Jeff Nauman at Bally Midway with a 'no wrong way to play' ethos.

links.took: Popularized playing an unstoppable giant scaling skyscrapers, smashing buildings, and swatting military choppers.
links.added: Translated side-view urban demolition into a free-roaming 3D sandbox with car-glove weapons and leap physics.
links.extra: Carried Rampage's playful city-smashing fantasy into 3D open-world action.

links.took: Julian Gollop's turn-based ZX Spectrum squad tactics with action points, line of sight, and sci-fi raids.
links.added: Rebuilt the engine in fast machine code with a larger scrolling map and a single-player computer opponent.
links.extra: Bridge between Gollop's 1984 debut and his 1988 hit Laser Squad.

links.took: Action-point squad movement, hidden enemy fog, and turn-based sci-fi firefights on scrolling maps.
links.added: Expanded into multi-scenario missions with custom weapon loadouts, destructible walls, and multi-system 16-bit releases.
links.extra: Julian Gollop's direct stepping stone from Rebelstar toward UFO: Enemy Unknown.

links.took: Yu Suzuki's into-the-screen Super Scaler sprite engine and full-body hydraulic arcade motion cabinet.
links.added: Swapped fantasy running for a supersonic F-14 Tomcat with radar lock-on missiles and barrel rolls.
links.extra: Built by Yu Suzuki and Satoshi Mifune on Sega's X Board hardware.

links.took: Fast-paced arcade fighter-jet dogfighting built around rapid radar missile locks and dramatic banking.
links.added: Moved supersonic air combat out of scaled rails into free-roaming 3D polygonal airspace and mission contracts.
links.extra: Namco's 1995 PlayStation debut launched the Ace Combat lineage.

links.took: Chuck Benton's 1981 adult-comedy text adventure plot, locations, and tongue-in-cheek puzzles.
links.added: Rebuilt it as an animated graphic adventure with Al Lowe's slapstick writing and an age-verification quiz.

src.t: Wikipedia: Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards

links.extra: Al Lowe pitched remaking Softporn Adventure to Ken Williams after Sierra lost its Disney license.

links.took: Sierra On-Line's AGI animated walking-character adventure engine and typed command parser.
links.added: Traded fairy-tale quests for a satirical Lost Wages lounge comedy with close-up character portraits.

src.t: Wikipedia: Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards

links.extra: Showed Sierra's adventure engine could power adult humor alongside fantasy.

links.took: Popularized aiming a physical optical light gun directly at moving on-screen targets.
links.added: Added horizontal rail scrolling, hostage protection, ammo management, and a mounted recoil-feedback submachine gun.

src.t: Den of Geek, The Unlikely Origins of the First-Person Shooter

links.extra: Popularized arcade military light-gun rail shooters across late-1980s and 1990s coin-ops.

links.took: Scrolling arcade light-gun rail shooting balancing hostile gunmen, reload timing, and civilian hostages.
links.added: Moved light-gun action into 3D Model 2 polygons with targeting reticles and limb-specific hit animations.
links.extra: Bridged 2D sprite light-gun cabinets and Sega's 3D arcade shooter wave.

links.took: A collectible power-up bar letting players choose movement and weapon upgrades mid-flight.
links.added: Turned horizontal shooting into a bouncing wizard orb and Catellite restoring stolen colors to monochrome landscapes.
links.extra: Jon Hare told Retro Gamer (2006) Wizball began as a Nemesis (Gradius)-inspired Commodore 64 shooter.

links.took: Sensible Software's crisp Commodore 64 sprite control, humor, and responsive arcade feel by Jon Hare and Chris Yates.
links.added: Pivoted from surreal color-restoration shooting to fast overhead soccer with banana-shot swerves and indoor modes.
links.extra: Jon Hare and Chris Yates followed Wizball with MicroProse Soccer, launching their Sensible Soccer and Cannon Fodder lineage.

links.took: Ryuichi Nishizawa's brisk arcade side-scrolling platform feel and charming fantasy protagonist.
links.added: Swapped skateboarding and axes for RPG towns, gold-dropping monsters, armor shops, and spell upgrades.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wonder Boy in Monster Land

links.extra: Pioneered arcade action-RPG platforming at Westone.

links.took: Fantasy RPG towns, equipment upgrades, gold economies, and tavern hint-gathering.
links.added: Compressed RPG progression into a real-time, timer-driven arcade side-scrolling platform adventure.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wonder Boy in Monster Land

links.extra: Director Ryuichi Nishizawa explicitly blended emerging RPG hits like Dragon Quest and Wizardry into arcade action.

links.took: Sword-and-shield platform combat, coin-funded equipment shops, and fantasy boss encounters.
links.added: Opened linear arcade stages into a non-linear world explored via six cursed animal forms with unique powers.

src.t: Wikipedia: Wonder Boy in Monster Land

links.extra: Direct sequel opening right after Monster Land's final dragon battle.

links.took: Realtime Games' experience adapting fast 3D vector flight combat for Rainbird on home computers.
links.added: Merged direct 3D piloting of amphibious tanks and jets with real-time strategic archipelago conquest.

src.t: Ian Oliver interview, Sega Retro / Bohemia Interactive, May 2012

links.extra: Ian Oliver and Graeme Baird coded the entire 3D polygon and RTS engine in 68000 assembly.

links.took: High-speed pseudo-3D scaling highways, branching forks, and racing against a ticking timer.
links.added: Turned scenic cruising into turbo-boosted police chases where players ram armed suspects off the road.
links.extra: Designed by Hiroguki Sakou on Taito's Z System arcade hardware.

links.took: Frantic timed street pursuits weaving through traffic to intercept and ram fleeing vehicles.
links.added: Expanded linear highway chases into four open 3D cities with wheelman physics and movie-style replays.
links.extra: Cited by historians as a key arcade precursor to Driver's urban pursuit design.

links.took: Aggressive high-speed weaving through oncoming traffic paired with violent vehicular ramming.
links.added: Built entire 3D arcade races around risky near-miss boost meters and slow-motion crash spectacle.
links.extra: Carried Chase H.Q.'s traffic-dodging ramming thrill into modern arcade racers.

links.took: Methodical horizontal alien-corridor shooting with biomechanical bosses and attachable defensive firepower.
links.added: Brought smooth 50 fps Amiga scrolling and token-collected weapon upgrades in DMA Design's debut release.
links.extra: First game programmed by David Jones in Dundee before DMA Design made Lemmings and GTA.

links.took: Lucasfilm's SCUMM point-and-click verb bar and switching between multiple playable characters.
links.added: Expanded a single mansion into a globe-trotting alien conspiracy spanning Earth, Mars, and psychic animals.

src.t: Wikipedia: Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders
David Fox interview, Popkulturowy Kociolek, Feb 2024

links.extra: Second title built on SCUMM, directed by David Fox with comedy polish suggested by Ron Gilbert.

links.took: Behind-the-car pseudo-3D scaling streets racing at high speed past traffic and tight turns.
links.added: Combined Batmobile street chases with grappling platform levels, Batcave chemical puzzles, and Batwing stages.
links.extra: Ocean Software's multi-genre tie-in became a blueprint for late-1980s European movie games.

links.took: Mechanical tether grappling to hoist a hero up vertical architecture instead of ordinary jumps.
links.added: Paired Bat-grapple traversal and Batarang fights with driving, flying, and deduction stages across Gotham.
links.extra: Transferred grappling-line platforming into Tim Burton's Axis Chemical Plant and Cathedral levels.

links.took: David Jones's smooth Amiga scrolling shoot-'em-up framework and alien stage bosses at DMA Design.
links.added: Added four distinct stage vehicles, an in-level coin weapon shop, two-player co-op, and blitter color depth.
links.extra: DMA Design's sophomore Amiga hit directly preceded Lemmings.

links.took: DMA Design's meticulous Amiga sprite animation pipeline and arcade-grade shooting polish.
links.added: Shifted from horizontal space vehicles to piloting a bipedal mech with mouse-aimed twin turrets.
links.extra: Blood Money's animation inspired Gary Timmons to join DMA Design and animate Walker.

links.took: Sierra On-Line's animated graphic adventure rooms, typed command parser, and fairy-tale humor.
links.added: Layered three RPG classes, skill leveling, real-time sword combat, and multiple class-based puzzle solutions.

src.t: Wikipedia: Quest for Glory: So You Want to Be a Hero

links.extra: Designed by Corey and Lori Ann Cole; later retitled Quest for Glory due to a trademark conflict.

links.took: Territory-conquest strategic maps resolved through brief real-time arcade combat minigames.
links.added: Brought two-player head-to-head rivalry, train robberies, fort assaults, and Belgian comic slapstick to the Civil War.
links.extra: Adapted by Infogrames from the Belgian comic strip Les Tuniques Bleues.

links.took: High-speed rear-view circuit racing balancing cornering lines against aggressive rival cars.
links.added: Built elevated 3D polygonal roller-coaster tracks with true suspension physics, drawbridge gaps, and nitro boosts.
links.extra: Geoff Crammond clarified he did not draw from Hard Drivin', seeing it only near completion.

links.took: Popularized pairing a top-down overworld map with side-scrolling action stages on the NES.
links.added: Let players swap on the fly between all four Turtles' distinct weapon reaches and rescue captured teammates.

src.t: Wikipedia: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (NES video game)

links.extra: Konami's 1989 NES hit also introduced pizza as the franchise's recurring health pickup.

links.took: Konami's NES Turtles cast, cartoon villains, and pizza health recovery items.
links.added: Pivoted from overworld platforming to dedicated two-player belt-scrolling brawling with signature special moves.

src.t: Wikipedia: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (NES video game)

links.extra: Continued Konami's home-console Turtles line after the 1989 NES debut.

links.took: Top-down divine world-shaping where miracles clear terrain and help fledgling human settlements grow.
links.added: Paired town-building god-sim phases directly with side-scrolling sword action stages and boss battles.
links.extra: Quintet's Super Famicom launch-window hybrid directed by Masaya Hashimoto with music by Yuzo Koshiro.

links.took: Deliberate gothic side-scrolling action stages culminating in mythic creature boss fights.
links.added: Linked every cleared action stage to an overhead simulation where growing towns power up the hero.
links.extra: Bridged classic Japanese 16-bit action platformers and Western god games.

links.took: Quintet's world-restoration themes, mythic storytelling, and snappy SNES action combat.
links.added: Unified action and story into a continuous globe-trotting action-RPG with three transformable forms.
links.extra: Second pillar in Quintet's unofficial SNES Heaven and Earth trilogy.

links.took: Flip-screen isometric dungeon rooms built around object-pushing and spatial puzzles.
links.added: Upgraded to 16-bit metallic pixel art, context-sensitive verb menus, and deep scripted item interactions.
links.extra: The Bitmap Brothers built Cadaver atop their custom Adventure Level Editor and ACL scripting language.

links.took: The Bitmap Brothers' signature metallic 16-bit tile craft, secret triggers, and tight room design.
links.added: Replaced solo isometric dungeon puzzles with fast two-player co-op steampunk top-down shooting.
links.extra: Mike Montgomery and Eric Matthews carried Bitmap Brothers' visual identity across both Amiga hits.

links.took: Expressive Disney character animation paired with bounce-based enemy stomping and hidden treasures.
links.added: Delivered lush 16-bit Genesis fairy-tale stages, thrown apple projectiles, and technical completion bonuses.

src.t: Wikipedia: Castle of Illusion Starring Mickey Mouse

links.extra: Directed by Emiko Yamamoto at Sega, setting the benchmark for 16-bit Disney platformers.

links.took: Yuji Horii and Chunsoft's expansive overworld questing, turn-based combat, and multi-character party.
links.added: Structured the story into five converging character chapters and introduced selectable AI battle tactics.
links.extra: Also introduced the party wagon, letting players swap reserve companions mid-journey.

links.took: Wagon party swapping, ensemble storytelling arcs, and AI-assisted companion battle commands.
links.added: Spanned three generations of one hero's life with marriage choices and recruitable enemy monsters.
links.extra: Direct continuation of Chunsoft's Zenithia trilogy.

links.took: Guiding AI-controlled party members via high-level tactical postures instead of every manual turn.
links.added: Turned fixed party tactics into granular, player-programmed conditional Gambit scripts in real-time combat.

src.t: Game Developer, The History of Dragon Quest

links.extra: Dragon Quest IV's Chapter 5 AI Tactics menu is widely noted as an early precursor to Gambits.

links.took: Four Warriors of Light, turn-based class combat, airships, and elemental crystal quests.
links.added: Introduced an on-the-fly Job System, summoned monsters, Moogles, and Square's Ether scripting engine.
links.extra: Directed by Hironobu Sakaguchi and programmed by Nasir Gebelli for the Famicom.

links.took: A swappable Job System letting four heroes change classes between battles.
links.added: Let characters retain learned active and passive skills across jobs for deep hybrid builds.
links.extra: Refined Final Fantasy III's job-swapping blueprint into a lasting JRPG customization template.

links.took: Capcom's gothic demon realm, grueling enemy patterns, and nemesis Red Arremer (Firebrand).
links.added: Made the gargoyle the hero with hovering flight, wall-clinging, and a top-down RPG overworld.
links.extra: Produced by Tokuro Fujiwara and designed by Kenshi Naruse for Game Boy.

links.took: Producer Tokuro Fujiwara's polished Capcom NES licensed platforming and non-linear stage exploration.
links.added: Replaced pogo traversal with feeding candy to dream creatures and wearing their digging and flying powers.

src.t: Wikipedia: Little Nemo: The Dream Master

links.extra: Designed by Tatsuya Minami with music by Junko Tamiya.

links.took: Acquiring distinct traversal and attack powers from stage creatures to solve platforming obstacles.
links.added: Streamlined creature abilities into instant inhale-and-copy powers across colorful floating platform stages.

src.t: Wikipedia: Little Nemo: The Dream Master

links.extra: Critics note Little Nemo's animal-power swaps anticipated Kirby's Adventure three years later.

links.took: Fast katana platforming, wall-clinging jumps, ninpo sub-weapons, and dramatic NES anime cutscenes.
links.added: Added full wall climbing, trailing shadow-clone doubles mirroring attacks, and wind, rain, and darkness hazards.

src.t: Wikipedia: Ninja Gaiden II: The Dark Sword of Chaos

links.extra: Directed by Masato Kato at Tecmo.

links.took: Technos Japan's big-headed Kunio-kun sprites, slapstick brawling physics, and knock-down tackles.
links.added: Moved Kunio onto a four-player NES soccer pitch with weather-slick turf and physics-defying super shots.
links.extra: Directly reused Kunio-kun character sprites from River City Ransom (Downtown Nekketsu Story).

links.took: Sega's 16-bit science-fantasy RPG universe, turn-based party battles, and icon menus.
links.added: Set the quest aboard a multi-biome generation ship with marriage choices spanning three generations and four endings.
links.extra: Its branching family tree predated Dragon Quest V's generational marriage storyline.

links.took: Sega's Genesis RPG engine conventions and sweeping multi-era Algol lore.
links.added: Added manga-panel cutscenes, combination attacks, programmable battle macros, and seamless town-to-dungeon flow.
links.extra: Co-directed by Rieko Kodama to close out the classic Algol saga.

links.took: Clean sci-fi RPG combat aesthetics, technique magic, and Hunters Guild quest framing.
links.added: Brought the franchise into 3D real-time Dreamcast action with four-player online lobby co-op.
links.extra: IGN highlighted Phantasy Star IV's accessible mechanics as a direct influence on Phantasy Star Online.

links.took: Nintendo EAD's SNES Mode 7 hardware scaling and rotation simulating 3D depth over flat maps.
links.added: Swapped high-speed racing for serene biplane, skydiving, rocketbelt, and hang-glider license tests.
links.extra: F-Zero launched with the Super Famicom in November 1990; Pilotwings followed one month later.

links.took: Scored aerial license challenges using hang gliders, rocketbelts, and precision target landings.
links.added: Replaced Mode 7 planes with full 3D N64 islands, gyrocopters, human cannonballs, and Little States sightseeing.
links.extra: Co-developed by Paradigm Simulation and Nintendo EAD for the Nintendo 64 launch.

links.took: Nintendo's breezy island flight school, skydiving rings, and tourist-island sightseeing loop.
links.added: Brought motion-controlled plane tours and skydiving onto Wuhu Island alongside twelve resort sports.
links.extra: Wuhu Island later hosted 2011's Pilotwings Resort, directly uniting both Nintendo series.

links.took: Sierra's three-class adventure-RPG hybrid, skill progression, and class-specific puzzle paths.
links.added: Let players import saved characters into Shapeir's day-night Arabian city with timed events and elemental battles.

src.t: Wikipedia: Quest for Glory II: Trial by Fire

links.extra: Designed by Lori Ann Cole and Corey Cole using Sierra's parser-driven SCI engine.

links.took: Accessible combat-flight dogfighting balancing historical theater immersion with approachable controls.
links.added: Brought 3D polygonal World War I biplane duels, rotary-engine torque, gun jams, and rival ace encounters.
links.extra: Created by Damon Slye at Dynamix for Sierra On-Line.

links.took: Core Design's trap-filled trial-and-error platform rooms and slapstick puzzle timing.
links.added: Traded Indiana Jones tombs for alien worlds with laser blasters, sliding bombs, and flying-disc stages.
links.extra: Designed and programmed by Simon Phipps at Core Design.

links.took: Will Wright's open-ended 'software toy' design and interlocking system feedback loops at Maxis.
links.added: Scaled simulation from one city to planetary tectonics, Gaia climate dynamics, and evolving species.
links.extra: Co-designed by Will Wright and Fred Haslam with Gaia theorist James Lovelock advising.

links.took: Will Wright's ambition to simulate planetary ecology and the rise of intelligent life at Maxis.
links.added: Swapped spreadsheet graphs for tactile creature editors and five playful stages from tidepool to galaxy.
links.extra: Will Wright's long-gestating return to SimEarth's evolutionary sandbox.

links.took: Isometric sloped obstacle courses and ledge physics from Rare's 1989 NES conversion of Marble Madness.
links.added: Swapped rolling marbles for two co-op snakes hopping across traps and eating pellets to weigh down exits.
links.extra: Wikipedia documents Snake Rattle 'n' Roll derived directly from Rare's NES Marble Madness port.

links.took: Nintendo's top-down NES action-adventure loop alternating overworld exploration with puzzle dungeons.
links.added: Created a Western-exclusive tropical chapter story featuring jumping dungeon tiles, baseball gear, and a yo-yo.
links.extra: Directed and written by Genyo Takeda of Nintendo R&D3 specifically for Western audiences.

links.took: Top-down miniature circuit racing with sharp drifting corners and multi-lap arcade pacing.
links.added: Added prize-money garages for upgrading engines, armor, front missiles, and rear land mines between races.
links.extra: Developed by Magnetic Fields (Gremlin) before their Lotus racing trilogy.

links.took: Popularized crisp top-down miniature car racing on 16-bit European home computers.
links.added: Shifted overhead circuits onto pool tables, breakfast counters, and bathtubs with knockout screen-scrolling multiplayer.
links.extra: Part of the vibrant British top-down racer wave on Amiga, ST, and NES.

links.took: Top-down cooperative maze shooting, key hunting, and relentless enemy swarms through narrow corridors.
links.added: Infused sci-fi horror atmosphere inspired by Alien with computer ammo terminals and claustrophobic lighting.
links.extra: Breakout Amiga hit for Team17, designed by Rico Holmes and produced by Martyn Brown.

links.took: Team17's high-contrast Amiga sci-fi art direction, heavy synth audio, and upgrade-shop polish.
links.added: Pivoted from top-down corridor horror to a punishing horizontal arcade shoot-'em-up.
links.extra: Cemented Team17's early-1990s reputation as an Amiga action powerhouse.

links.took: Modern jet-fighter cockpit combat simulations across multi-mission military campaigns.
links.added: Pushed PC fidelity with real-simulator F-16 aerodynamics, padlock target view, wingman orders, and dynamic wars.
links.extra: Designed by Gilman Louie and Les Watts at Sphere for Spectrum HoloByte.

links.took: Popularized realistic 3D cockpit instrument flying and aerodynamic modeling on personal computers.
links.added: Applied math-coprocessor flight physics to F-16 radar avionics, air-to-air missiles, and dynamic war theaters.
links.extra: Falcon 3.0 set a new 1990s high-water mark for civilian-PC military flight realism.

links.took: Geoff Crammond's custom 3D polygonal vehicle physics and smooth home-computer frame rates.
links.added: Delivered a realistic 16-track Formula One season with cornering telemetry, racing lines, and optional driving aids.

src.t: Wikipedia: Formula One Grand Prix (video game)

links.extra: Known as World Circuit in North America; set the benchmark for 1990s PC sim racing.

links.took: Geoff Crammond's rigorous Formula One handling model, millisecond timing, and scalable driving aids.
links.added: Added official 1994 FIA licensing, texture-mapped 3D circuits, engine and gearbox failures, and active modding.
links.extra: Geoff Crammond's DOS sequel became a pillar of PC sim-racing communities.

links.took: The Bitmap Brothers' shaded metallic Amiga pixel art, lever puzzles, and compact inventory management.
links.added: Shifted to side-scrolling mythic Hercules platforming featuring adaptive AI that rewards skilled play with secret rooms.
links.extra: Designed by Eric Matthews and Steve Tall with a Nation 12 soundtrack.

links.took: Bullfrog's isometric land-raising god game pitting rival tribes of worshipers across islands.
links.added: Expanded from eight powers to thirty Greek-myth elemental miracles, wandering heroes, and earned skill points.

src.t: Wikipedia: Populous II: Trials of the Olympian Gods

links.extra: Designed by Peter Molyneux and Glenn Corpes at Bullfrog Productions.

links.took: Sir Arthur's two-hit armor loop, treasure-chest weapons, and unforgiving gothic action stages.
links.added: Introduced Arthur's signature mid-air double jump, magic-charging gold armor, and SNES Mode 7 rotating chambers.
links.extra: Directed by Tatsuya Minami and produced by Tokuro Fujiwara as the series' first console-native entry.

links.took: Procedurally generated floors, hidden passages, and unidentified items you risk opening to learn their effects.
links.added: Reimagined dungeon crawling as a split-screen funky Genesis co-op hunt for spaceship pieces.

src.t: Greg Johnson interview, Mega Visions, Mar 2019

links.extra: Greg Johnson played mainframe Rogue until 4 a.m. in college and built ToeJam & Earl on its loops.

links.took: Deliberate, one-hit-kill arcade side-scrolling pacing where enemy timing matters more than speed.
links.added: Turned a cursed warrior into a slow-moving ape spitting upgradeable fireballs, helmets, and jumping boots.
links.extra: Developed by TAD Corporation (former Data East staff) in 1989 arcades before widespread 1991 home ports.

links.took: Piloting a combat helicopter behind enemy lines to destroy threats and airlift stranded hostages.
links.added: Expanded rescues into open isometric Gulf campaigns juggling finite fuel, ammo, armor, and multi-stage targets.
links.extra: EA founder Trip Hawkins specifically suggested Mike Posehn build a game inspired by Apple II Choplifter.

links.took: Relentless side-scrolling run-and-gun blasting, weapon power-ups, and multi-directional aiming.
links.added: Adapted A New Hope with three playable heroes, lightsaber swings, and Mode 7 landspeeder and X-Wing stages.
links.extra: Built by Sculptured Software and LucasArts with John Williams's score arranged for the SNES sound chip.

links.took: Isometric four-car combat racing with missile pickups and cash-bought engine and tire upgrades.
links.added: Added sloped alien tracks, licensed classic rock arrangements, and enthusiastic race announcer Larry Huffman.
links.extra: Developed by Silicon & Synapse right before the studio renamed itself Blizzard Entertainment.

links.took: Grid-maze block blasting, chain-reaction bomb blasts, and flame-range power-ups.
links.added: Bundled with the SNES Multitap, making four-player couch battle arenas and sudden-death closing walls a staple.
links.extra: Published by Hudson Soft and developed by Produce! in 1993.

links.took: Popularized graphical PC storytelling structured around exploring rooms and solving thematic puzzles.
links.added: Replaced text parsers with pre-rendered 3D mansion walk-throughs, 21 logic puzzles, and streamed CD-ROM actors.
links.extra: Built by Rob Landeros and Graeme Devine at Trilobyte, driving early PC CD-ROM adoption alongside Myst.

links.took: CD-ROM haunted-mansion horror combining pre-rendered interiors with filmed live-action actors.
links.added: Shifted from abstract board puzzles to a seven-CD cinematic psychological thriller directed by Roberta Williams.
links.extra: Part of the mid-1990s CD-ROM full-motion-video horror wave.

links.took: Popularized top-down two-player maze shooting against relentless swarms of varied monsters.
links.added: Traded dark fantasy dungeons for B-movie suburbia rescues armed with squirt guns, silverware, and weedwackers.
links.extra: Designed by Mike Ebert at LucasArts with music by Joe McDermott and George Sanger.

links.took: The four 1981 arcade stages where Mario climbs girders and dodges barrels to rescue Pauline.
links.added: Unfolded into 97 acrobatic Game Boy key-and-switch puzzle levels with handstands, backflips, and bridge blocks.

src.t: VG247, Daily Classic: Donkey Kong's Game Boy Reinvention, Feb 2014

links.extra: Produced by Shigeru Miyamoto; laid the puzzle-platformer blueprint for Mario vs. Donkey Kong.

links.took: MicroProse's tile-grid world map, turn-based city management, and historical grand-strategy loop.
links.added: Focused tightly on New World colonies with raw-to-finished trade chains, specialist citizens, and an independence war.
links.extra: Co-designed by Brian Reynolds and Sid Meier at MicroProse.

links.took: Yu Suzuki's three-button punch-kick-guard 3D martial arts duels and ring-out arenas.
links.added: Moved onto Sega Model 2 hardware with texture-mapped fighters, motion-captured animations, and 60 fps fluidity.
links.extra: Added drunken-fist master Shun Di and praying-mantis fighter Lion Rafale.

links.took: Hard-hitting Sega Genesis side-scrolling combo brawling and urban enemy waves.
links.added: Staged fights directly inside comic-book panels where Sketch Turner rips paper planes and puzzles across gutters.

src.t: Sega-16, Developer's Den: Sega Technical Institute, Jun 2007

links.extra: Conceived by Peter Morawiec at Sega Technical Institute.

links.took: Fast first-person corridor combat, colored key hunts, shareware distribution, and moddable archive files.
links.added: Replaced 2.5D flat planes with true polygonal 3D mines, full six-degrees-of-freedom flight, and reactor escapes.

src.t: Game Informer, The Secret History of Volition, Mar 2011

links.extra: Directed by Parallax Software co-founders Mike Kulas and Matt Toschlog.

links.took: Parallax Software's 3D cockpit engineering, smooth polygonal rendering, and mission-focused combat feel.
links.added: Left claustrophobic zero-G mines for vast fleet-scale space wars with power routing and subsystem targeting.

src.t: Wikipedia: Descent: FreeSpace – The Great War
Game Informer, The Secret History of Volition, Mar 2011

links.extra: Built by Volition after Parallax Software split into Volition and Outrage Entertainment.

links.took: Sega's forward-moving rail shooter structure dodging hazards and blasting incoming aerial formations.
links.added: Added 3D Saturn dragon flight, 360-degree camera rotation, multi-target homing lasers, and a Moebius-inspired world.

src.t: Game Developer, The History of Panzer Dragoon, Apr 2008

links.extra: Directed by Yukio Futatsugi at Sega's Team Andromeda.

links.took: Team Andromeda's post-apocalyptic dragon lore, 360-degree camera awareness, and homing-laser combat.
links.added: Rebuilt the Saturn shooter as a 3D RPG where players orbit enemies across four tactical combat quadrants.
links.extra: Directed by Yukio Futatsugi with on-the-fly dragon stat morphing.

links.took: Quintet's top-down SNES action-RPG structure, Mode 7 overworld travel, and cosmic rebirth storytelling.
links.added: Accelerated spear combat with dashing and jumping attacks as Ark resurrects continents, ecosystems, and civilization.
links.extra: Directed by Tomoyoshi Miyazaki as the climax of Quintet's unofficial Heaven and Earth trilogy.

links.took: Revolution Software's Virtual Theatre engine with independent wandering NPCs and clean context-sensitive mouse controls.
links.added: Upgraded to hand-drawn animated cinema visuals for a globe-trotting Knights Templar thriller in Paris.

src.t: Wikipedia: Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars
GamesIndustry.biz, Can you solve the mystery of the Broken Sword?, Nov 2005

links.extra: Directed by Charles Cecil with animation led by former Don Bluth artists.

links.took: Popularized witty, fair point-and-click adventures centered on conversation trees and logical inventory puzzles.
links.added: Replaced text verb lists with direct context-sensitive clicking and hand-animated European conspiracy storytelling.

src.t: Wikipedia: Broken Sword: The Shadow of the Templars

links.extra: Helped keep 2D point-and-click adventures thriving across PC and PlayStation in the mid-1990s.

links.took: Kirby's floating platform traversal and inhaling enemies to copy their signature powers.
links.added: Expanded each copy ability into multi-move directional arsenals, co-op Helpers, and seven distinct anthology modes.

src.t: Masahiro Sakurai, Kirby Super Star SNES Classic Interview, Nintendo, Oct 2017

links.extra: Directed by Masahiro Sakurai and produced by Satoru Iwata at HAL Laboratory.

links.took: Masahiro Sakurai's accessible directional fighting-style movesets, crisp menus, and boss choreography at HAL Laboratory.
links.added: Turned single-button plus direction combat into a four-player Nintendo crossover platform fighter.

src.t: Masahiro Sakurai, Kirby Super Star SNES Classic Interview, Nintendo, Oct 2017

links.extra: Sakurai pivoted straight from Kirby Super Star into prototyping Super Smash Bros. at HAL.

links.took: Psygnosis's futuristic airbrake anti-gravity racing, weapon pads, and club-culture graphic design.
links.added: Smoothed wall-scraping physics, added ship destruction, pit-lane shields, and licensed Prodigy and Chemical Brothers tracks.
links.extra: Released as Wipeout XL in North America; grew out of a planned track add-on.

links.took: Westwood Studios' high-production PC storytelling, atmospheric audio, and custom software-rendering craft.
links.added: Built a real-time voxel detective adventure with autonomous NPCs, ESPER photo scanning, and randomized replicants.
links.extra: Executive-produced and coded by Westwood co-founder Louis Castle with composer Frank Klepacki.

links.took: Popularized mouse-driven point-and-click adventures centered on dialogue, clues, and atmospheric storytelling.
links.added: Dropped verb bars for a live real-time noir world, Voight-Kampff empathy tests, and thirteen branching endings.
links.extra: Told an original parallel 'sidequel' intersecting Ridley Scott's 1982 film.

links.took: Ken Silverman's Build engine, interactive room-over-room geometry, and wisecracking first-person gunplay.
links.added: Added voxel props, real-time shadows, dynamite bundles, pitchforks, and macabre gothic-horror camp.
links.extra: Started under 3D Realms before Monolith Productions acquired the rights and shipped it in 1997.

links.took: Cultist backwoods horror atmosphere, occult shotgun-and-pitchfork arsenals, and brisk 1990s shooter pacing.
links.added: Combined Build-engine folk-horror vibes with Quake's bunny-hopping speed and acrobatic 3D verticality.
links.extra: Blood became a touchstone of the late-2010s retro 'boomer shooter' revival.

links.took: High-tension Japanese sword duels where spacing, feints, and single clean slashes outweigh combos.
links.added: Removed health bars, timers, and arena walls in favor of limb injuries, stances, and one-hit kills.
links.extra: Directed by Kunihiko Nakata at Lightweight as a 'swordsmanship simulator' for PlayStation.

links.took: Sega's Model 2 3D polygon light-gun rail shooting, off-screen reloads, and hostage rescues.
links.added: Swapped static gunmen for charging undead hordes, destructible limbs, boss weak points, and branching routes.

src.t: Wikipedia: The House of the Dead (video game)

links.extra: Directed by Takashi Oda at Sega AM1; became Japan's top-grossing arcade cabinet of 1998.

links.took: Full 3D polygonal first-person shooter arenas, vertical architecture, and fast weapon switching.
links.added: Brought console analog-stick FPS navigation, platforming leaps, bows, and hunting dinosaurs to Nintendo 64.
links.extra: Designed by David Dienstbier at Iguana Entertainment, arriving months before GoldenEye 007.

links.took: Top-down mouse-driven control of a small vulnerable war squad across detailed hostile terrain.
links.added: Inverted arcade gunfire into methodical WWII puzzle-stealth built around enemy vision cones and patrol timing.

src.t: Jon Beltran de Heredia (Pyro Studios) interview, Arcade Attack, Mar 2020

links.extra: Designed by Gonzalo Suarez and Ignacio Perez Dolset at Madrid's Pyro Studios.

links.took: Asymmetric puzzle design requiring distinct non-overlapping character tools to clear each bottleneck.
links.added: Scaled specialist cooperation to six WWII commandos coordinating disguises, lures, sniping, and demolitions.
links.extra: Sparked the real-time tactics stealth subgenre later revived by Desperados and Shadow Tactics.

links.took: Popularized stealth infiltration built around dodging enemy patrol routes and avoiding lethal alarms.
links.added: Turned solo espionage into real-time isometric six-specialist WWII tactics with visible enemy sight cones.
links.extra: Adapted stealth patrol reading into a tabletop-like overhead tactical puzzle.

links.took: Energy shunting between shields, engines, and weapons alongside crisp starfighter dogfight and escort missions.
links.added: Added subsystem targeting, directional hull collision physics, and towering Shivan capital ships in an original setting.

src.t: Wikipedia: Descent: FreeSpace – The Great War

links.extra: Volition cited TIE Fighter and Wing Commander as primary inspirations for FreeSpace's flight model.

links.took: Volition's power-shunting space combat engine, wingman orders, and Shivan interstellar conflict.
links.added: Scaled up to colossal capital-ship beam duels, sensor-scrambling nebulae, and an enduring open-source mod engine.
links.extra: Widely regarded as the peak of 1990s PC space-combat simulations.

links.took: Ultra-fast futuristic hovercraft cornering, boost management, and recharge pit strips.
links.added: Trimmed scenery to run 30 racers at 60 fps across twisting 3D pipes, loops, and spin attacks.
links.extra: Directed by Tadashi Sugiyama and produced by Shigeru Miyamoto for Nintendo 64.

links.took: A modified Final Fantasy VII PlayStation engine, Active Time Battle pacing, and cinematic pre-rendered scenes.
links.added: Fused real-time movement dodging and firearm customization with a six-day Manhattan biological horror thriller.

src.t: Kotaku, Parasite Eve Had More In Common With Final Fantasy Than Horror Games, Oct 2016

links.extra: Directed by Takashi Tokita and produced by Hironobu Sakaguchi as a 'cinematic RPG'.

links.took: Pre-rendered urban survival-horror corridors, police-protagonist framing, and mutating biological monsters.
links.added: Replaced tank-control aiming with Active Time Battle domes, RPG leveling, and weapon stat tuning.
links.extra: Sequel to Hideaki Sena's 1995 horror novel, bridging PlayStation JRPGs and survival horror.

links.took: Namco's subterranean digging premise, crushing boulders, and Dig Dug hero Taizo Hori's lineage.
links.added: Turned underground tunneling into a frantic color-matching puzzle descent racing against falling blocks and oxygen.

src.t: Retronauts, Dig Dug & Mr. Driller, Jul 2017

links.extra: Yasuhito Nagaoka originally drafted the 1998 prototype as Dig Dug 3 before Hideo Yoshizawa reshaped it.

links.took: tri-Ace's fast action-leaning JRPG combat sensibility, voice-acted battles, and multi-ending narrative craft.
links.added: Paired Norse soul-reaping chapters and side-scrolling platform dungeons with four-button combo-juggling turn combat.
links.extra: Directed by Yoshiharu Gotanda and designed by Masaki Norimoto with Motoi Sakuraba's score.
